warmup.text: Hangtown at last. Before you read, think about why Praiseworthy keeps slowing Jack down. Then read a six line poem about an eagle, twice. It may be about more than one thing.

words.text: Today you hunt for openers and transitions, the words that link one idea to the next. Find the fort and val roots in new words. Then spot the endings that name ideas. Six more pans to wash.

reading.text: Read Chapter 11, Jamoka Jack. The diggings are not what Jack imagined. Watch what Jack is willing to do to be accepted, and watch what Praiseworthy has to give up along the way.

assignment.text: Three questions about Chapter 11. Then turn your plan into sentences. If you get stuck, use the frames on the card. Name a character's choice, and say what it shows.

cards.title: Real history: Hangtown and the dry washers
cards.intro: Pitch-pine Billy and his friends are made up. Hangtown was a real gold camp, and the history below is real.

items.term: A real town with a hard name
items.meaning: Miners first called the camp Dry Diggings, because they carried the dry dirt down to water to wash out the gold. In 1849 a crowd there hanged three men accused of robbery, without a real trial. After that, people called the camp Hangtown. Many people did not like the name, and in 1854 the town took a new one: Placerville, the name it still has.

Pitch-pine Billy says dry washing is a trick from Sonora, Mexico. That part is true. Miners from Sonora, where water is scarce, knew how to get gold out of dry dirt, and thousands of them came to California in 1849.

In 1850 California made miners who were not American citizens pay $20 a month to dig, a huge sum then. It fell hardest on Mexican and other Latin American miners, and many were driven from the mines. The law was ended in 1851.

items.term: Each camp made its own rules
items.meaning: There was no state mining law yet. In each camp the miners met and voted on their own rules: how big a claim could be, how to mark it, and how often you had to work it to keep it. Billy's rules in Chapter 11 are the novel's version.

cards.note: Sources: City of Placerville; California State Parks, Historical Landmark No. 475; Calisphere, University of California.

virtue.name: honesty

options.t: On the stage, Praiseworthy tells the road agent he is “Not a gentleman. Merely a butler.”
In Hangtown, Praiseworthy writes to Dr. Buckbee that Cut-Eye Higgins is in town and the map was taken by highwaymen.
Praiseworthy tells Pitch-pine Billy, “The name is Praiseworthy, not Butler, sir.”

art.title: Gold Mining in California
art.alt: A colored print of miners in red shirts working a mountain stream: one pans for gold, two shovel dirt into a long wooden trough, and others work a hillside, with a cabin, pine trees and snowy peaks behind.
art.look: A hand-colored print by Currier and Ives, sold in 1871. It shows many ways of washing gold at once: a miner crouches with a pan in the stream, two men shovel dirt into a long trough, and up on the hill others wash the bank with a hose, a method from the later years. Find the pan. That is how Pitch-pine Billy teaches Jack in Chapter 11.
